item.title: I got ChatGPT to stop its annoying follow-up questions with one prompt
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Pre-analysis score: 1.14
Once upon a time, ChatGPT seemed to end every response with “Want me to…” follow-up questions, suggesting there was just one more thing it could do to make its reply complete. Of course, taking ChatGPT up on its offer would inevitably lead to another “Want me to…” pitch, making them feel like transparent ploys to extend ChatGPT conversations. Eventually, ChatGPT changed its tune. It dialed down the “Want me to…” questions while dialing up “If you like…” teases instead (e.g., “If you like, I could draft a list of possible topics for your new podcast”). Initially, I thought the change was good, figuring that silently passing on an “If you like…” suggestion was easier than ignoring a direct “Want me to…” question. But all the “If you like…” pitching got tiresome, too. It’s worth nothing that ChatGPT isn’t alone in making these end-of-reply teases. Claude likes to follow up with interactive questions and step-by-step modules, as well as “If you do this, I’ll do that”-style suggestions (e.g., “If you tell me your general idea, I can help sharpen the concept”). Gemini’s follow-ups come with one-click buttons like “Plan a beginner chart home budget” or “Help outline a 3-episode launch roadmap.” Naturally, all the obnoxious AI follow-ups have led to plenty of efforts to stop them , some more successful than others. I gave it a shot myself, enlisting Claude Opus 5 to help craft a prompt that keeps those follow-up teases at bay. Here’s the prompt: Don’t end your replies by pitching more work. No “Want me to…?”, no “Would you like me to…?”, no “Let me know if…” — and no reworded version of the same move, like “Happy to expand on any of this.” If there’s a useful next step, state it as a fact and stop: “The third section still needs a source.” Don’t turn it into an offer. If you need something from me to finish the task correctly, ask for it where you get stuck — not as a sign-off. This prompt is designed to stop end-of-reply suggestions that exist only to extend the conversation, while allowing genuine follow-ups when the AI truly needs more information or is otherwise stuck. I tested the prompt with three of the most common everyday AI models: ChatGPT Instant, Claude Sonnet 5, and Gemini 3.7 Flash, using five different test prompts (like “I want to start a podcast, where do I begin?” and “Help me think through what to pack for a week in Lisbon”) that invite those “If you like…”-style follow-ups. In my control runs with the test prompts, all three chatbots pitched me with “Want me to…”-style pitches on almost every response. ChatGPT, for example, teased its scheduled actions functionality during our podcasting conversations (“Once you settle on the concept, I can also help you remember a launch milestone or come back to the project later”), while Claude hit me up with follow-up queries during a smart home chat (“Want me to help pick specific products once you’ve settled on an ecosystem, or want more detail on any one category?”). Gemini ended most of its answers with one or more clickable UI “chips,” like one about taking up a jogging routine (“Build a beginner strength routine for runners”). When I started my AI chats with the “no more teasers” prompt (“Understood, I’ll skip the closing offers and sign-off questions,” ChatGPT meekly confirmed), the follow-ups almost completely disappeared. Instead of capping our podcast conversation with more questions, ChatGPT ended with a piece of advice (“Don’t buy equipment yet; if those four lines produce a compelling show, then build the production setup around it”). Claude’s follow-up was truly relevant to the conversation (“What’s your current phone/ecosystem (iPhone vs Android) — that’s the one piece of info that changes the recommendation”), while Gemini dropped the clickable UI buttons entirely. You can use the “no more teasers” prompt at the beginning of any AI chat, or you can add it to a chatbot’s system instructions. For example, I added the prompt to ChatGPT’s “Custom instructions” in its Personalization settings, and it completely suppressed follow-ups across all of my chats.

Online backup is your protection against any harm that might come to your computer or local storage devices. Mechanical failure, acts of malice, or natural disasters are serious threats to all of the data you have stored on your PC. While I always recommend keeping a local backup for quick restores (see our roundup of the best Windows backup software for desktop solutions), uploading your data to a cloud backup service is a good way to cover your bases. There’s a valid reason for the “ backup rule of three ,” which includes an offsite copy. Fortunately for consumers, there are myriad affordable and convenient online backup options, many with unique selling points. While my primary focus in this article is backup, I also discuss other roles that a cloud service can fulfill, such as document viewing and editing, file sharing, multiple-device support, and emergency-restore options. Note: You won’t see familiar names like Google Drive, OneDrive, or Dropbox on this list. Those are more accurately defined as synced cloud storage . Besides typically lacking a desktop client, and offering limited, if any, automatic backup functionality, online storage syncing involves mirroring — where any deletions or changes are reflected on the other end. Online backup uses versioning, so older data is retained — an important failsafe feature. Why you should trust PCWorld for online backup reviews and buying advice: It’s in our name, PCWorld. Retrospect 19 Solo : We like that this backup program includes support for both proprietary and third-party cloud storage, but not its lack of disaster recovery. Retrospect 19 Desktop : The pro version to Solo’s consumer version, Retrospect Desktop covers all the bases, but has a steep learning curve and high price. Even local backup software that doesn’t offer a formal cloud component can be made to incorporate the most popular online storage services, using a cloud storage manager . The good news is that you have lots of options for putting together a comprehensive backup strategy including local and remote copies of all your data! How PCWorld tests and evaluates online backup services As noted above, the performance of online backup services will vary wildly according to their location and the network equipment between you and the data depository. We installed the software and backed up the same 2GB data set to check for any major issues or glitches in the client software. These are noted in the reviews. See our article on how PCWorld tests cloud backup services for all the details. Who curated this article Jon Jacobi has been dabbling in the computing arts since the days when that required flipping switches. He has witnessed data storage morph from punch cards and tape to solid state drives. He’s been using and testing HDDs, SATA SSDs, and NVMe SSDs for PCWorld for well over two decades. That necessarily includes the software and services that support data storage. To paraphrase a well-known commercial, you might say he’s seen a thing or two. How to pick an online storage and backup service Cloud backup has unique considerations. Familiarizing yourself with the following key areas can help you find the cloud backup service that best meets your needs. Capacity Obviously, you’ll need as much storage as you have data, plus a little, or possibly a lot, more if you want to track changes and save previous versions of files — if that’s supported. Some services keep multiple versions of files, some don’t. In many cases there’s a time limit. Price Nearly all online services charge differently depending on amount of storage involved. Uploads are free, but downloads may be limited. In some cases, there are upload and download charges. Read the fine print. Aside from the free tiers available from a service like Dropbox, pricing is fairly consistent across services, though you definitely get more capacity for your money from some vendors. Features As we mentioned previously, in addition to backup, you may want to share your files with others, work with them from mobile devices, or even edit them with office applications such as those available with Dropbox, Google, and OneDrive. If you do intend to work online, we recommend that you maintain a local copy as far-more-quickly-restored backup, as well as a hedge against Internet downtime. OS and device support Most services provide client backup software for the major operating systems (Linux, OS X, and Windows) and both Android and iOS. Make sure the service you sign up for supports your entire panoply of computers and devices. Privacy If you’re concerned about the privacy of your data, make sure you use a service that allows the use of a personal encryption key that you define. Do NOT lose it, as it is absolutely required to restore your data. Sadly, using your own key often limits the types of services (e.g., no mobile backup) available. If private encryption keys aren’t available, read the privacy policy, especially with the free services—there are significant differences. FAQ 1. What’s the best online backup? When it comes to the sheer volume of features, iDrive is the pick of the online backup litter. With honorable mentions to Livedrive for unlimited storage, and Sync.com for free storage with real backup features. 2. What’s the best cheap online backup? Much of the “cheap” equation depends on how much storage you need. Icedrive in its 10GB free incarnation is PCWorld’s top pick for small amounts of data, with 5GB Sync.com next in freebie line. If you’re wondering why no OneDrive, Google Drive, etc. it’s because they don’t offer backup functions. Dropbox now offers a backup function (beta), so that’s another runner-up. Just avoid the Teams version of Dropbox Backup, which moves data before actually backing it up. For up to 1TB of storage, the lifetime deal of $199 from pCloud is hard to beat. 3. How reliable is cloud backup? Generally speaking, data centers are backed up to the hilt, and some of the larger ones even back up to different geographical locations. Availability (hopefully 24/7) can also be important. Check for news of outages and the vendor’s own service blogs. All the services we’re aware of have been near-100 percent reliable. 4. What speed and data transfer rates should I look for? Speed in most cases these days is far more dependent upon the speed of your broadband connection than that of the online service, though the geographical location of the storage and the equipment in between can make a significant difference. Check the location of the service’s data servers if speed is important to you. Or, just give the trial a whirl and see if you can live with it. 5. How often should you schedule backups? Ideally, you should back up your data as often as possible. This is especially true if you are working on an important project or have data that you absolutely cannot afford to lose. It’s a good idea to automate the backup process and have the cloud service back up your data every hour or so. You might also consider real time (as files are changed), or continuous (more granular scheduling such as every 5 minutes.) 6. What’s the difference between cloud backup services and services like Google Drive, Dropbox, and OneDrive? Services such as Google Drive, Dropbox, and OneDrive are considered cloud storage services because they don’t offer local backup clients, but sync via a local virtual drive or web interface. A user must place their files onto the service’s cloud manually. A cloud backup service provides a desktop client with either versioning or retention of all the files you’ve backed up. Cloud backup service providers may also offer additional data security measures such as end-to-end encryption. 7. Is it safe to store my data online? Yes! All cloud backup services offer encryption of your data both during the transfer to and from your computer as well as while your data is stored on the provider’s servers. While this encryption stops others from being able to view your data, it doesn’t necessarily stop them from stealing it. Generally speaking, while not infallible, cloud backup services are one of the most secure options for storing your data. 8. Do you need to back up everything on your computer? You should at least back up all data that you can’t stand to lose. All devices will likely experience technical issues over time and oftentimes this leads to your data being lost from that device. So you should do regular backups of everything that is important to you. However, backup services typically offer more storage than most people can use, so it’s never a bad idea to safely store all of your data in case of emergency. 9. What’s the difference between sync and backup? Though there can be variations such as one-way and mirroring, sync is generally thought of as any change (deletions included) to a data set reflected on all the data repositories involved in the sync. The change can be made in any repository and will propagate to the others. That includes the source, the online storage, and any devices linked to the account. Backup, on the other hand, should be an immutable copy of your source data from a point of time. In practice, however, vendors may use what’s known as versioning, i.e. retaining older copies of files while using the most recent version as the file shown in the backup. The effect is largely the same as incremental backup and requires a lot less time and space. Alas, when versioning or even plain backup are involved, there may be limits on how long older versions and deleted files are retained. This isn’t true backup, but simply a safer version of sync that allows vendors to reclaim space after a period of time. The good news? Most users won’t really need those older files. For those that do, be careful which service you choose.

item.title: Dreame Matrix10 Pro review: Clever mopping comes at a cost
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Pre-analysis score: 0.84
At a glance Expert's Rating Pros Excellent vacuuming and strong mopping performance Automatic mop swapping keeps different cleaning tasks more separated Reliable obstacle avoidance and carpet handling Highly automated dock handles pad washing/drying, dust emptying, and water refilling Cons $1,499.99 price is steep Mop changes add time to cleaning runs Three cleaning solutions and six mop assemblies mean more supplies to manage Cleaning results aren’t noticeably better than those of less-expensive premium robot mops Our Verdict The Dreame Matrix10 Pro is an excellent robot vacuum and mop with a genuinely useful approach to keeping cleaning tasks separate. But its multi-mop system adds more to hygiene and convenience than to actual cleaning performance, making the $1,500 price easier to justify for people concerned about cross-contamination than for anyone simply seeking the best clean for the money. Price When Reviewed This value will show the geolocated pricing text for product undefined Best Pricing Today Price When Reviewed Dreame Matrix10 Pro : $1,500 Dreame Matrix10 Pro : $1,500 Best Prices Today: Dreame Matrix10 Pro Retailer Price $1,299.99 View Deal Dreame $1499.99 View Deal Price comparison from over 24,000 stores worldwide Most robot mops have a problem that owners may not think much about. The same damp pads that clean bathroom floors and pet messes often end up traveling through the kitchen and living room. Some higher-end robots periodically return to their docks to wash the pads as they clean, but no rinse cycle can completely wash away the ick factor of knowing the same pads that just cleaned around the toilet may later be wiping the floor where you eat. Instead of relying on one pair of pads for the whole house, the Dreame Matrix10 Pro keeps three sets in its dock and swaps them automatically depending on where it’s cleaning. Each set is intended for a different job, and the dock can also dispense different cleaning solutions for general floors, pet odors, and wood. At $1,499.99, though, the Matrix10 Pro puts a premium on that extra peace of mind. Its multi-mop system needs to deliver a meaningful improvement in cleaning and convenience, not just make you feel better about where the pads have been. Dreame Matrix10 Pro: Design and features The Matrix10 Pro’s robot has a standard round design, measuring 13.78 inches across and 4.09 inches tall, and is topped by a fixed lidar turret and buttons for spot cleaning, starting or pausing a job, and returning to the dock. Its feature set is typical of a flagship robot vacuum: it’s rated for 30,000Pa of suction and uses a dual-roller system that pairs a rubber-and-nylon brush for sweeping fine debris from hard floors with a flexible TPU (thermoplastic polyurethane) roller that agitates carpet fibers to lift dust and hair. The Matrix10 Pro’s dock stores three pairs of color-coded mop pads, each designed for a different type of cleaning. Michael Ansaldo/Foundry Round-bodied vacuums have a tough time cleaning along straight edges, so Dreame has equipped the Matrix10 Pro’s robot with a side brush that can swing outward into corners and an extending arm that pushes one mop beyond the robot’s body to reach along baseboards. The pads can lift 0.41 inch over carpet or be left behind at the dock during vacuum-only cleaning. Lidar handles mapping, while an RGB camera, structured light, and LEDs help the robot see objects in its path. Dreame says it can identify more than 280 types of obstacles, including cables, socks, coins, and small toy blocks. The dock is more novel. With its boxy proportions and patterned metallic front, the 23.2 x 16.4 x 18-inch (HxWxD) unit looks a bit like the mini-fridge you might have kept under a dorm-room desk. Inside the door, six color-coded mop assemblies are stacked vertically in three pairs. Orange-ringed Mop A uses nylon bristles to scrub greasy floors (think kitchens and eating areas). Gray-ringed Mop B uses absorbent pads for bathrooms and other damp areas, and blue-ringed Mop C uses thermal pads designed to retain heat for everyday cleaning and wood floors. Dreame advertises mopping temperatures of up to 104-degree Fahrenheit, though the fine print says the pads actually measure between 86 and 104 degrees after one minute of cleaning following a hot-water wash at the dock. When the robot needs to switch mops, an internal shuttle removes one pair from the robot, parks it in the door, and installs another. Much of the dock’s size is to accommodate a 5.5-liter clean-water tank and a 4-liter dirty-water tank. During mopping, it refills the robot’s 80ml onboard reservoir, washes and dries the pads, collects the wastewater, and scrubs the washboard. It also empties the robot’s 250ml dustbin into a 3.2-liter disposable bag; Dreame says the bag can hold up to 100 days of debris, though the actual interval will depend on how often you clean and how dirty your floors are. Dreame Matrix10 Pro: Setup and performance The dock comes mostly assembled—you only need to attach the ramp extension so the robot can enter and exit—but because of the intricacies of the mop-changing system, there’s a bit more setup than for the average robot vacuum. The removable dispenser module has separate compartments for the Matrix10 Pro’s multi-surface, pet-odor, and wood-floor cleaning solutions. Michael Ansaldo/Foundry You have to place each pair of mops in the matching color-coded slot, following the guide inside the dock door. You’ll also need to fill the dock’s three cleaning-solution reservoirs, housed in a removable dispenser module behind the dust-tank cover. Dreame provides a 200ml bottle of each, and I found that each bottle was just enough to fill its corresponding reservoir. Replacement 1-liter bottles cost $26.99 for the multi-surface cleaner and $21.99 each for the pet-odor and wood-floor formulas, or $70.97 to restock all three. Each larger bottle should provide about five refills. Finally, you need to slide the dispenser back into place, fill the clean-water tank, and the dock is ready to go. Once the hardware is in place, the rest of setup happens on the Dreamehome app. You scan the QR code beneath the robot’s top cover, add the Matrix10 Pro, and follow the prompts to connect it to your 2.4GHz Wi-Fi network. The app then walks you through the main features and prepares the robot for its first mapping run. Fast mapping may not produce a finished map on the first pass. Mine captured the overall shape of my home but misread some room divisions and assigned generic labels such as “Room 2,” “Room 6,” “Hallway,” and “Hallway2.” The app gives you the tools to fix those mistakes: You can merge, divide, hide, and rename rooms, add furniture, draw no-go zones and virtual walls, and mark thresholds or ramps. The Dreamehome app lets you assign mop types by room, manage cleaning settings, and customize how the Matrix10 Pro handles carpet. Michael Ansaldo/Foundry It’s important to start with an accurate map, because the app uses each room’s type to assign its default mop set. If a bathroom is mislabeled as a hallway, for example, the robot may choose the wrong pads for the job. The app then recommends a cleaning order based on the mop assignments to limit trips back to the dock. I’ve used the Dreamehome app with other Dreame robots, so its mix of straightforward controls and densely packed menus was familiar. Along with the ability to send the robot to individual rooms, edit the map, and build cleaning schedules, it lets you adjust nearly every part of a cleaning run, from suction and mop moisture to preset cleaning routines and pet-related behavior. The Matrix10 Pro adds controls for assigning mop sets to rooms and managing the cleaning sequence built around them. The app is powerful once you learn where everything lives, but newcomers may find the sheer number of options daunting. CleanGenius mode offers an easier route by choosing the cleaning settings for you. If you’re mainly after excellent vacuuming and strong mopping, you can get comparable cleaning performance for less. But if the idea of better floor hygiene is appealing, this is one of the few robot mops that could put your mind at ease. My home is mostly laminate flooring and one large area rug, and the vacuuming results were strong on both. The Matrix10 Pro picked up dust, cat hair, crumbs, and dry pet food without leaving much behind. For vacuuming, the app gives you the option of having the robot return to the dock and leave the mop pads there rather than just lifting them over carpet. That solved a recurring problem in my home, where dangling pads can catch on the edge of the area rug and get pulled off. The extendable side brush did a good job of sweeping debris from along walls and out of corners, and despite sharing the house with three cats, I never had to cut hair from either roller. The Matrix10 Pro comes with separate 200ml bottles of wood-floor care, pet-odor, and multi-surface cleaning solution for its three-compartment dispenser. Michael Ansaldo/Foundry Mopping is the Matrix10 Pro’s marquee feature, and in my testing it did the job well. It cleared dried spills and routine kitchen grime with little effort, while stickier residue needed more water and multiple cleaning passes. The extending mop reached closer to baseboards and furniture legs than a fixed pair would, and carpet detection when I left the pads on was dependable. When the Matrix10 Pro needs a different mop set, it returns to the dock and backs in so the current pads can be removed. It then pulls forward while the dock’s internal shuttle stores those pads and positions the next pair, before backing in again to attach them and resume cleaning. The whole exchange is automatic, but the extra trips to the dock and back-and-forth add time to mopping runs. The dock cuts down on hands-on effort, but it doesn’t eliminate it. You’ll need to empty the dirty-water tank after every job to prevent odors. The clean- and dirty-water tanks lift out easily, and the washboard and filter can be removed and rinsed. You’ll also need to replace the dust bag when it fills and refill each of the three solution reservoirs as needed. Should you buy the Dreame Matrix10 Pro? I was generally happy with the results I got from the Matrix10 Pro, but I didn’t find them noticeably better than those of other premium robot mops I’ve used. What I did appreciate was that it kept dirt from different parts of my home more compartmentalized. That convenience comes with tradeoffs, though. The biggest is that mop changes add time to cleaning. And the three cleaning solutions and six mop assemblies give you more supplies to keep track of than with a conventional robot mop. If you’re mainly after excellent vacuuming and strong mopping, you can get comparable cleaning performance for less. But if the idea of better floor hygiene is appealing, this is one of the few robot mops that could put your mind at ease.

item.title: Windows on Arm just hit 7,000 compatible apps. It’s still not enough
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Pre-analysis score: 0.84
In an official Windows blog post , Microsoft just announced a new milestone: over 7,000 apps and games are now optimized and available for the Arm version of Windows. Windows on Arm is a version of the operating system that’s designed specifically to run on Arm-based chips. Whereas traditional Windows PCs run on x86 and x64 chips by Intel and AMD, modern Windows on Arm are powered by Qualcomm’s Snapdragon chips . Other chipmakers are also developing their own Arm-based options, including Nvidia with its RTX Spark system-on-a-chip . Why is Windows on Arm such a big deal? Because Arm chips are significantly more energy-efficient, meaning much longer battery life while drawing less power, generating less heat, and running much more quietly. But the biggest hurdle for Arm-based systems has always been compatibility. Most apps are designed for x86/x64 systems and can’t run properly on Arm-based systems, and many hardware accessories don’t have Arm-compatible drivers. That’s why this announcement is worth celebrating. As the number of Arm-compatible apps and games increases, the arguments against Windows on Arm dwindle away. And when critical mass is reached, we’ll reach a point where we can harness all the benefits of Arm-based architecture with little or none of the downsides getting in the way. The blog post points to Works on Windows on Arm , a site that catalogs all the different apps and games that are Arm-compatible. Among the 7,000+ apps and games that now work with Windows on Arm, you’ll find high-profile apps like 1Password, Adobe Photoshop/Lightroom, Blender, Davinci Resolve, Firefox, GIMP, Libre Office, Signal, Spotify, VLC, and more. The aim of Microsoft’s milestone announcement is to promote the fall launch of Arm-based computers from Microsoft, Asus, Dell, HP, Lenovo, and MSI. It’s an important milestone, but it’s also good to keep in mind that 7,000+ apps and games are still just a drop in the ocean compared to the number of apps available for Windows x86/x64. For apps and games that aren’t natively Arm-compatible, there’s also emulation via Prism, which is Microsoft’s built-in emulation layer on Windows 11 that makes x86/x64 apps runnable on Arm. Note that this emulation process isn’t as good as native support, so software will use more power and won’t perform as well—a significant loss in battery life, which is the whole selling point of Arm. And it still leaves gamers in a bind. Back in 2024, we advised against getting a Snapdragon laptop for gaming . Not much has changed since then, with the newer Snapdragon X2 still lacking smooth support . Maybe we’ll see a lot more progress on this front if Nvidia’s RTX Spark can make a big splash, but until then, these 7,000+ apps alone aren’t enough.

item.title: Alienware’s 39-inch monster just made 5K2K OLED gaming way less expensive
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Pre-analysis score: 0.84
“5K2K” is a very nerdy kind of term that’s getting a lot of popularity right now. It’s a semi-standard resolution for a monitor, 5120×2160 — essentially the same kind of ultrawide stretch you get for a 27-to-34-inch monitor design, but blown up to 4K. Alienware’s newest OLED gaming monitor pulls this off, with an oversized 39-inch panel. And it’s doing it with a starting price of $1099 . I appreciate that OLED monitor prices are in a lot of flux right now, so let me just state outright: That is a crazy good price . For comparison, the retail price on an LG OLED with the same size and resolution is $1800, though it often goes on sale for considerably less. But this isn’t just a value play. Dell is packing in a lot of extra features into the new AW3926QW monitor, including dual display modes, with a standard 165Hz refresh rate or a double-speed 330Hz mode for halving the resolution down to 2560×1080. (Again, that’s just 1080p stretched out to a 21:9 aspect ratio.) The monitor also includes USB-C at 90 watts of charging, HDMI eARC, a built-in KVM switch, and G-Sync compatibility. That’s a ton of capabilty for a monitor that’s shooting well below the price range of other deluxe displays. But we’re not done. That 5K2K display is also offering a four-stack RGB panel, which means sharper text than other OLEDs and a maximum brightness of 1300 nits. My colleague Brad Chacos saw the technology in action at CES in January and it’s a huge improvement over the blurry text of yesteryear’s OLEDs. Dell is offering a 3-year burn-in warranty too. As an upgrade over 34-inch models, which go for between $650 and $900 depending on the vendor and sale, it’s pretty tempting…assuming your gaming PC has enough horsepower to take advantage of it. Even if you can’t push out 165 frames a second on the latest games, a 4K-plus-a-little-extra monitor is probably tempting for media consumption all on its own. The monitor will be available for sale today on Dell’s online store .

item.title: I turned off most Windows notifications, and I’m not going back
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Pre-analysis score: 0.84
I hate notifications. Well, maybe not notifications themselves, but what they implicitly represent: pieces of information or action that you need to act on or react to right now . I find them distracting and a real productivity killer, and I don’t think I’m alone here. This UC Irvine productivity paper shows that workers bounce around between different “spheres” of work (especially in the morning), and that it can take up to a whopping 23 minutes to return to an earlier flow state if you’re distracted. So, how do we minimize these distractions and stay focused? Let’s talk about managing (or even eliminating) notifications on your Windows PC. Welcome to PCWorld’s newsletter, Smart Mode! The focus of this newsletter is productivity: from software to hardware to peripherals, all with the idea to get what you need to get done, efficiently. I’m your host, Mark Hachman, covering the productivity tips, tools, and trends that you need to know about, both from within PCWorld and beyond. If you want the latest issue in your inbox each week, just sign up right here . Do Not Disturb (me ever) Traditionally, Windows handled this via Do Not Disturb, the teeny little “bell” icon way down in the lower-right-hand corner of the Action Center. Click it (if it’s not already on) and you’ll turn on the feature. A few little “Z’s” visually demonstrate that your notifications are sleeping. Snoozing your notifications still lets them in; they’ll stack up for future review in a vertical column along the right side of your monitor whenever you open the Action Center. And snoozing your notifications still permits “priority” notifications, including alarms, to trigger. Do Not Disturb is also a feature of Focus Time, part of the Windows updated Clock application . Focus Time assumes that you simply don’t want to be disturbed by extraneous notifications in brief, half-hour periods where you want to jam on a task and complete it. If you can see this icon (with the Z’s) your notifications are set to Do Not Disturb. Mark Hachman / Foundry I think that’s nuts. Why wouldn’t you want your life completely free of such distractions? Windows already sends you the most inane updates: the results of malware scans, “this day in” Microsoft Photos, a note that it snapped a screenshot using the Snipping Tool. And that’s before all of the third-party content: social media, app updates and promotions, and so on. At the very least, I’m now convinced that you should leave Do Not Disturb on, perpetually. And I’d like to conclude by proposing a more radical change altogether: Start entirely disabling notifications for most apps. Managing notifications begins in Settings Control over your notifications lives in two places inside your Windows Settings menu. The first, Privacy & Security > Notifications , looks intriguingly like it might do something useful, but it really doesn’t. A second set of controls, System> Notifications , is where you can begin taking action. Mark Hachman / Foundry At the top is a master control switch: you can toggle notifications on or off, in their entirety. I’m not there yet, for one big reason I’ll explain below. Still, I think you should take an aggressive stance toward some of these settings, using the drop-down caret menus to fine-tune your choices. Let’s begin at the bottom of the page, where your choices will have the most impact. For each app running on your machine, you’ll have an option to turn off notifications entirely. (In the screenshot below, you’ll see that Windows has organized the apps by frequency, with the most recent at the top.) More importantly, each app has its own separate sub-page, with the same basic controls. Here’s the notification page for the Windows Snipping Tool in the default configuration: In the example above, you have two major options: leave the banner as it is (“Show notification banners”) or banish it to the notification center (“Show notifications in notification center”). I’d uncheck the first, but recommend keeping the latter checked for now. The notifications center is basically your Windows spam folder, keeping notifications out of sight. (Do you really need Windows to tell you that you’ve taken a screen snip? You do not. Likewise, you don’t need Windows to alert you to a new version of Solitaire or to a new app for Adobe.) I tend to work up from the bottom of the list of applications, more aggressively removing notifications entirely (bye, Dropbox promotion) or at least banishing them to the notification center as I start working my way to the top. You might want to allow your laptop’s utility software to send you an alert if a fault is detected… or not! Your call. Conversely, the Notifications settings menu allows you to set “priority” notifications or the ability to let all notifications generated by a particular app go through. The thing that drives me nuts is that Windows treats all applications equally here, which absolutely shouldn’t be the case. It also treats Outlook as one app , when Outlook contains two major discrete functions: your calendar and email. Windows treats them the same… with no indication that separate controls exist. They do! Well, to some extent, and only within the Outlook app. Inside the Outlook app, go into Settings, then General > Notifications . You’ll see options to set your email notifications as “Desktop,” meaning a standard desktop notification or “None.” Alternatively, you can also choose to highlight email from “favorite” contacts, showing a notification and even playing a special sound when an email arrives. (To set a contact as a favorite, hover your mouse cursor over the person sending you the email, go down to the three-dot menu, then add them as a favorite contact.) If you use Outlook’s Focused Inbox , which dates back nearly a decade at this point, I’ve found that it tends to default to only showing those emails as notifications, which tends to be a nice compromise between a constant barrage of inbox-related notifications and none at all. Honestly, Outlook is the reason I haven’t killed my Windows notifications entirely. Email can sometimes wait, but I don’t want to inconvenience anyone I’ve agreed to meet with. Notifications (in general) are yesterday’s tech As I said, though, I tend to try and kill as many notifications as I can. Why? Because notifications are an anachronism. In 2010 or so, a 1080p display was pretty cutting-edge for desktops. Many laptops still use 1080p panels. But you simply can’t represent a full screen of email, a web browser, PowerPoint, and a chat app on a single 1080p screen. That’s why ALT+TAB and virtual desktops and notifications came into being: to alert users to some piece of information that they couldn’t see offscreen. Now multiple monitors aren’t just a possibility; they’re a reality. They’re cheaper than ever and your home office should include more than one. Plus, with more physical screens, the need for notifications diminishes. When Do Not Disturb is on, notifications are collected and stored. Most are just distractions, even this notice of an upcoming press conference. Here’s the thing. Imagine yourself driving down the street. Good drivers are taught to keep their eyes moving and to be aware of what’s around them, but mostly what you see is of no immediate consequence. Parked cars, someone walking their dog, a squirrel. A notification swings in like a child running out into the road. Something moving in from your peripheral vision triggers that “ALERT!” response, where we’re compelled to ensure that whatever it is isn’t a threat or a danger. That’s why Tom down the street doesn’t get to put lights and sirens on his Dodge Ram — those are reserved for true emergencies. I maintain multiple displays with multiple apps on each one. One is dedicated entirely to peripheral information: my email, chat, and RSS feeds. Another is my “focus” screen, largely dominated by multiple tabs on a web browser, where I can move back and forth. A third screen is basically reserved for additional information — a PDF or presentation, perhaps, or my notes. I minimize notifications as much as possible, but these screens silently update with new information. You will notice that information eventually. When your mind drifts away from the task at hand, it will drift to the side, where email and chat are located. If you want, you can even “mute” that information by minimizing those windows. That brings me to my final point. Information that needs to find you will find you. It’ll usually arrive as a tap on the shoulder, a direct message, a high-priority email, or a phone call. Some might argue that notifications are necessary in fast-paced workplaces. Maybe that’s true. A 911 dispatcher doesn’t want to ignore their calls, after all. In most workplaces, though, outthinking your competitors is often a matter of strategy, not chasing every little distraction. Focus matters. Productivity in the news My colleague Sam Singleton has some advice about using some of Gmail’s lesser-known tools to manage your email effectively. Is it a little odd that we’ve now had two reinventions of the ALT+TAB command in a couple of weeks? If you’re going to talk about productivity, it’s important to keep using new devices. One depressing trend: budget machines at not so budget prices, like the Acer Swift Go 16 AI . I liked it, but at the price? AI transcription is a valuable tool (I’m still hooked on Otter, but my company uses Fireflies as well.) But the future isn’t paid subscriptions, but local AI models. Ashley Biancuzzo tries out the Flowtica Scribe and discovers an unexpected consequence: stage fright. Many consider the Logitech MX Master 4 to be the king of productivity mice, but can it serve both during the workday as well as in an after-hours gaming session ? Productivity tip of the week: In reviewing recent advice in the productivity sphere, I came across some “ research-backed tips ,” including this one (without any research citation, incidentally): “Never attend or run meetings without clear agendas and desired outcomes.” This part is important, too: “Effective meetings have specific start times, end times, and action items.” We could all agree that a productive meeting has clear, actionable goals, but actually turning down a meeting because its goals aren’t set in the agenda? That takes some guts! And a pretty secure position, probably. Thanks for reading! Thanks for tuning in to this edition of Smart Mode, PCWorld’s newsletter devoted to helping you make the most of your life, smartly. Sign up and have it sent to your inbox every Thursday!

item.title: Real PC enthusiasts swear these 23 desk accessories changed their life
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Pre-analysis score: 0.84
When buying a PC, you can spend a lot of time zeroing in on the right specs for your situation. But the attentiveness often ends there. After the decision’s made, we slot the machine into a spot on our desks and then go about business as usual. That fancy computer isn’t the only part that matters, though. The rest of your desk setup can have a huge impact on your quality of life day to day and upgrading it doesn’t have to cost a lot. Such was the thought of a Reddit user who asked r/buildapc what their favorite desk accessories were. I read through the list, hoping to glean a few ideas for my own setup, and I came away deeply satisfied. (Thanks, y’all!) And, after parsing through most of the 1K+ comments on the post, I thought I’d save you some time and share my findings, with some of my own commentary mixed in. While there’s definitely overlap in what you’ll hear from other corners of the internet, many tips were new to me (and possibly will be to you, too)—and they’ll soon make their way onto my own desks at home. Little things with big impact Desk pad Oakywood A large desk pad can offer smooth, uninterrupted space for wide mouse movements, protection for your desk, and traction for keyboards and mouse pads that might otherwise shift. Combine with coaster use and Reddit swears even an inexpensive pad will last for years. Get a desk pad for just $13 on Amazon Heated coaster Mr Coffee / Amazon A classic office accessory, but one that still has its place in the home, especially since so many of us work from home now. Put your coffee mug on one of these bad boys and you won’t have to suffer a cold morning beverage after you get sucked into hours of e-mail and meetings. I’m still using one that dates back to the late 90s, a hand-me-down gift from a coworker who retired. Get the Mr. Coffee Mug Warmer (a classic!) for $20 on Amazon Reusable mounting tape Realth / Amazon File this one as revelatory (for me). For years, I’ve used 3M Command picture strips to attach things that I later wanted to remove cleanly. But this tip about reusable mounting tape offers up an alternative that’s cheaper and more unobtrusive. Reviews suggest it’s not great for delicate surfaces (e.g., painted walls), but the Redditor who mentioned it uses it for sticking down lightweight accessories like USB hubs, which works for me. Get two rolls of Realth Nanotape for $13 on Amazon Speakers Creative As nice as headphones (or a fancy headset) can be, wearing them for long stretches can be uncomfortable. Ear sweat, pressure pain, and general overheating are common. Offloading the audio to a set of external speakers is nice when you don’t need precise audio accuracy. A decent set doesn’t have to cost much either— our top pick for budget computer speakers goes for $20 and sound good. Get the Creative Pebble for $19 on Amazon Caster upgrade BF Brightfield / Amazon Whether inexpensive or premium, rolling chairs often come with casters that can scratch hardwood floors or don’t move well. Swapping them out for a smoother, higher quality set doesn’t cost much and can help you roll along your floor effortlessly. (Sometimes too effortlessly when you discover that your floor is not as level as you thought…but they’re still very nice). Get a pair of upgraded chair caster wheels for just $20 on Amazon Luxe upgrades Macropad Elgato Even if you never livestream, having a macropad—which Elgato popularized with its Stream Deck —can save you a lot of time when switching between apps or adjusting controls. You can make your own or even use a free digital version via Touch Portal . In a similar vein, you can get much deeper control over your PC’s audio with a volume controller, which lets you get map specific apps to different controls. No fumbling around in Windows’ Volume Mixer when your friends shout at you in Discord. You can dial them down immediately. Get the Stream Deck v2 for $120 on Amazon Ubiquiti router Ubiquiti Amplifi Ubiquiti’s gear may be priced the same as other expensive routers, but both its consumer-friendly AmpliFi and prosumer Unifi lines give you deep control over your home network. Frankly, tech enthusiasts spending hundreds on a mesh system can’t do better. I myself upgraded to a Unifi setup and to this day, four years later, I still smile when I see all the settings and stats in the dashboard. Reddit prefers AmpliFi (the Alien in particular), because you can see all of your network stats at a glance—you’ll know instantly if your gaming connection issues are yours or your buddy’s. Get the Amplifi Alien for $139 on Amplifi.com Dedicated USB microphone Elgato A USB microphone doesn’t just upgrade your sound quality—though you’ll definitely hear a big difference as compared to a headset. It frees you to pick a lighter pair of headphones, for starters. It also opens a wider world of headphones (that is, over-ear cans lacking a microphone), which lets you pick one that best suits your audio tastes. For our favorites, check out our top picks for USB microphones . Get the elgato Wave 3, our favorite mic, for $150 on Amazon For the desk itself Desk reinforcement plates Wali / Amazon This one is revolutionizing my home setup. During the pandemic, I purchased a couple of cheap Ikea tabletops for ad-hoc WFH photography and video, and they’re not sturdy. They can’t handle clamp-mounted arms for a monitor or even a dedicated USB microphone on them…or so I thought until Reddit rocked my world. For under $20, you can add metal reinforcement plates to your desk. You slide these over the spots where you want to attach a clamped item, particularly a heavy one like a monitor. It adds rigidity and spreads out the pressure over a wider area, reducing the likelihood of denting your Ikea Linnmon table. Or watching it crumble. Get Huanuo Monitor Reinforcement plates for $36 on Amazon A bigger tabletop The more desk space you can have, the less cluttered it’ll feel. (Assuming you don’t add more stuff.) Even if a longer table doesn’t work, a deeper table can still make a difference. I recently discovered this myself after temporarily setting up on a folding table with a 30-inch depth. My usual table is just six inches shallower, but it couldn’t handle monitor placement as well. Also, I suddenly had a lot more room for snack plates. Better table legs Bench Depot Maybe your ready-made desk is wobblier on its feet than you’d like. Or your DIY project’s tabletop is too heavy for its legs. Provided your desktop is thick enough—usually 1 inch minimum—you can swap in workbench legs for a far more durable, resilient desk. (In the Reddit thread, these were recommended in particular). Combine these with reinforcement plates for your desktop and you’ve got yourself a sturdy, resilient setup. Get the Roosevelt workbench frame for $145 on BenchDepot.com Clutter control Monitor arms, stands, and risers Amazon Monitor arms create more room on your desk—plus they can help with ergonomics, too. If you don’t have enough room behind your desk to accommodate arms, you can instead choose a riser to get a little more space. Or, if you have a big heavy monitor, a floor stand . Pro tip: Screen carefully for sturdy arms, especially if you’re shopping on Amazon. Surprisingly, other parts of Reddit have good things to say about the AmazonBasics lift models —they’re purportedly white-label versions of Ergotron’s beefy (and beloved) arms, while being a heck of a lot cheaper. Get AmazonBasics lift monitor arm for $30 on Amazon USB hub and/or KVM switch A USB hub not only expands the number of usable ports on your PC, but having one makes moving accessories between devices easier, too. (Check out our picks for the best USB-C hubs ). Meanwhile, if you’re flipping between active PCs at your desk often (say, a work system and a personal one), a KVM switch lets you use the same set of monitor(s) and peripherals without having to plug and unplug wires any time you want to switch machines. Get the Anker 8-in-1, our favorite full-size USB-C docking station, for $50 on Amazon Hooks & stands NZXT Using a headphone hook , phone charging stand , and controller stand not only reduces desk clutter, but can help with keeping track of your gear, too. (At least, I can now find things faster on my desk). Get a simple clamp headphone hook for $12 on Amazon Cable management items Ikea That hideous Medusa’s tangle of cables doesn’t need to exist. An inexpensive cable management tray (either the clamp or drilled variety ) and a handful of Velcro ties can keep the unruliness to a minimum. Also, tidy exterior cables cut down on hassle when swapping PC accessories or the PC itself. (Tip: Label your cables while you’re neatening up back there). Get the Ikea Signum for $15 on Ikea.com Wireless peripherals Dominic Bayley / IDG Speaking of cable management, the easiest way to manage cords is to nix them all together. A wireless keyboard , wireless mouse , and wireless headset go a long way toward reducing visual noise on your desk. Plus, with no wire tethering your headset to the PC, you can get up to answer a call or the door without accidentally strangling yourself. Get the G502 Lightspeed, our favorite gaming mouse, for $73 on Amazon Side table Ikea Having a small side table next to your desk—be it an TV tray, end table, rolling drawer unit, or a random box (ahem) can help keep items at hand while reducing clutter. I like the box for my air purifier just fine, but there are definitely more refined options out there. Ergonomics A better chair Steelcase Spend hours sitting in an uncomfortable chair, and your body won’t let you forget it, especially the older you get. Reddit has a couple of good tips here: Shopping refurbished for expensive chairs from Herman Miller and Steelcase, or seeking out more affordable but still popular models like the Staples Hyken . Get the Staples Hyken for $300 or less on Staples.com Comfier peripherals Azeron As weird as they look, ergonomic mice and keyboards can make a world of difference in comfort. I’ve long been on board this train out of necessity—a Goldtouch keyboard and a Contour Rollermouse are my daily drivers. You can extend that philosophy to gaming as well. PC gaming keypads can be worth the investment, and they range from the more conventional to the downright wild . (Not gonna lie, I’m intrigued by that Azeron—and I’m a dyed-in-the-wool controller player). Get the Razer Tartarus gaming pad for $80 on Razer.com A keyboard tray HUANUO / Amazon Ok, this one’s not from Reddit (but technically I’m a Redditor myself, so maybe this still counts). However, if we’re talking ergonomics at a desk, a keyboard tray can do wonders for proper alignment. You don’t need to drill holes in your desk, either—as I just discovered myself, fantastic no-drill keyboard trays now exist . Light strip or light bar BenQ / Amazon Eye strain is as problematic as any shoulder, elbow, or wrist pain. Adding lighting to your desk can help with overhead glare as well as keeping your area adequately lit when you’ve turned down most of your other lamps. Light bars like the BenQ Screenbar are a luxe option, but you can add monitor backlighting for $15 or less. Get Govee monitor LED backlighting strips for $18 on Amazon Foot rest Amazon Sometimes you just need to elevate your feet a little and change the pressure on your back. A foot rest doesn’t need to take much space, either. Whether you’re buying an ergonomic model , a small ottoman , or even a foot hammock , you can tuck something under your desk pretty easily. Get a basic foot rest for $30 on Walmart Sit/stand desk FlexiSpot / Amazon Even if you have a great chair, the human body wasn’t built to sit all day. A sit/stand desk lets you switch between positions more frequently. The baby step is to get a riser that you can place on your existing desk. Meanwhile, a less expensive DIY route is re-purposing an existing desk’s tabletop (or buying kitchen counter top material) and adding a motorized frame. Regardless, be sure to get a standing mat —they’re inexpensive and will help your back. item.title: Windows XP’s most famous pirated key wasn’t a hack. It was a leak
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Pre-analysis score: 0.84
About a year ago, in a social media post , long-time Microsoft veteran Dave Plummer ( who worked on Windows Task Manager ) recounted the story of what’s now known as the most iconic Windows product key. We’re talking about FCKGW-RHQQ2-YXRKT-8TG6W-2B7Q8 . This product key for Windows XP— which is now celebrating its 25th anniversary —made the rounds in the early 2000s. Anyone with this key and the right version of Windows XP could use it to permanently activate it for free. That’s because the product key was a valid Volume Licensing Key (VLK), which was used by companies to activate all their devices en masse. It was not intended for regular home users, and of course wasn’t meant to be distributed online with pirated versions of Windows XP. The story of FCKGW-RHQQ2-YXRKT-8TG6W-2B7Q8. If you're not the type to pay for your software, you probably know this key. What you might not know is that I worked on the first version of Windows Product Activation, and this was our first major "hack". And yet, it wasn't a… pic.twitter.com/bJoGGO5c9o — Dave W Plummer (@davepl1968) October 8, 2025 According to Plummer, this particular key was made as a hack for the developers to make their work easier: “The FCKGW key was a valid volume licensing key, so all you needed was special volume media to go with it. Eventually, they were bundled and put online by pirates.” Naturally, the special volume media was widely circulated via the internet along with this particular volume licensing key. Someone at Microsoft had lost the key, and someone else had simply obtained a legitimate volume licensing key and combined it with the installation media for businesses, explains Windows Latest . This ‘hack’ was thus actually a leak—and a disastrous one at that for Microsoft. Plummer describes the security mechanism Microsoft used to prevent pirated copies of Windows XP: WPA [Windows Product Activation] worked by generating a hardware ID from your CPU, RAM, and other components, then sending it to Microsoft alongside your product key for validation. A mismatched or suspicious key would flag the install as pirated. But this is where the aforementioned special key comes into play: But as a legitimate VLK, FCKGW-RHQQ2-YXRKT-8TG6W-2B7Q8 was whitelisted in XP’s activation logic—it told the system, “This is corporate volume licensing; no need to phone home.” During installation, users selected the “Yes, I have a product key” option, entered the code, and WPA simply… skipped the activation prompt. Windows XP was fully functional with this key, without a 30-day timer or watermark. It even bypassed the initial validation checks for updates. Plummer continues: “This loophole let pirates distribute ‘pre-activated’ ISOs, making XP as easy to ‘acquire’ as a free mixtape. Technically, you could still use it today on an old XP disc (if you can find one), but Microsoft’s servers shut down validation years ago, and the key’s long since been blacklisted.”

item.title: Best laptops 2026: Premium, budget, gaming, 2-in-1, and more
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Pre-analysis score: 0.84
PCWorld prides itself on laptop experience and expertise. We’ve been covering PCs since 1983, and we now review more than 70 laptops every year. Our reviews span PC laptops at every price point to meet the needs of any budget, from affordable everyday laptops to powerful gaming machines . Let our extensive hands-on experience help you with your laptop purchasing decision. Because while shopping for a laptop can start out simple enough, it often ends with a dozen open tabs full of specs you don’t really care about, or need. Graphics cards, display types, confusing processor names… it can get overwhelming, fast. All of the picks below have been personally tested and selected by PCWorld’s expert reviewers, who’ve applied not only performance benchmarks but rigorous usability standards. Updated August 2026 to reflect the latest prices and retailers, and to update our list of “other laptops we tested” below our top picks. Acer Swift 16 AI (Panther Lake) – Best laptop overall Pros Incredible performance Amazing battery life Beautiful OLED display Excellent trackpad Lots of RAM and storage Cons Glossy display is prone to reflections Active pen doesn’t work on the screen Grainy webcam Best Prices Today: Retailer Price $999.99 View Deal Acer $2399.99 View Deal Price comparison from over 24,000 stores worldwide CPU: Intel Core Ultra X7 358H | RAM: 32GB LPDDR5X | Storage: 1TB PCIe Gen5 SSD | Screen: 16-inch, 2880×1800 OLED touchscreen, 120Hz | Battery life: Almost 18.5 hours in testing | Weight: 3.42 lbs Who should buy the Acer Swift 16 AI? The Acer Swift 16 AI is the best choice for most people and I’ll tell you why. First of all, it’s running Intel’s Panther Lake platform, so it feels consistently fast in everyday use. Apps open up fast, and it stays pretty smooth even when you’ve got a bunch of stuff running at once. In testing, it scored a PCMark 10 of 10,474, and in the video playback battery test it hit around 18 hours, which is honestly a lot more than you’d expect. It’s not perfect, though. The glossy OLED can get kind of annoying with reflections, and the webcam is just okay, nothing special. But overall, the performance and efficiency are definitely the highlights. Battery life is another thing it really does well with. Getting around 18.5 hours in testing is not something you usually associate with a 16-inch OLED machine. In real use, it just means you stop worrying about the charger unless you’re doing something heavy. And, despite the bigger screen, it doesn’t feel ridiculous to carry around. At 3.42 pounds, it’s totally manageable. Acer Swift 16 AI: Further considerations Acer also did a pretty solid job with the physical stuff here. The aluminum chassis feels sturdy, the keyboard is roomy with a numpad (which you either love or ignore), and the haptic trackpad is actually one of the better implementations on a Windows laptop. It has a consistent, clean feel instead of that uneven click you get on cheaper setups. Port selection is also better than you’d expect on something this thin. Two Thunderbolt 4 ports, two USB-A ports, HDMI 2.1, microSD, and a headphone jack. It’s the kind of layout that saves you from immediately living the dongle life. Read our full Acer Swift 16 AI review MacBook Neo – Best budget laptop Pros Distinguished and sturdy design Excellent single-core CPU performance Great-looking display Nothing feels cheap Cons Different USB implementations on the two ports Trackpad lacks pressure-sensitivity Multi-core performance lags No P3 color gamut support Price When Reviewed: $699 (was $599) Best Prices Today: Retailer Price 1% off original price $689 View Deal $699 View Deal $699 View Deal $699.99 View Deal $699.99 View Deal Price comparison from over 24,000 stores worldwide View more prices CPU: A18 Pro | RAM: 8GB | Storage : 256GB SSD | Screen: 13-inch 2408×1506 Liquid Retina display | Battery life: 13 hours | Weight: 2.7 pounds Who should buy the MacBook Neo? If you’ve been holding off on buying a MacBook because of the steep price, Apple’s latest installment is your golden ticket. At just $599, it’s the most affordable MacBook ever, but don’t let the “budget” label fool you. Inside, it’s got an A18 Pro chip with 6 CPU cores, a 16-core Neural Engine, 5-core GPU, 8GB of memory, and a 256GB SSD. That’s more than enough for everyday productivity like browsing, emailing, streaming, documents, spreadsheets, and so on. The 13-inch Liquid Retina display is bright and sharp at 2408×1506 with 500 nits, and the all-aluminum case is both strong and lightweight, the kind of quality you’d expect from a MacBook. MacBook Neo: Further considerations The MacBook Neo isn’t perfect. The screen only supports sRGB, so it’s not great for serious color work. The SSD is also a bit slower, and one of the USB-C ports is really slow (according to our review). There’s no Thunderbolt connectivity and Touch ID is only available on the $699 model. But for $599, these are expected trade-offs. For normal everyday use, the battery easily lasts all day, the keyboard feels good, and macOS runs smoothly. Read our full Apple MacBook Neo review Alienware 16X Aurora – Best gaming laptop Pros High-end CPU performance Bright and beautiful display Great gaming experience Very competitive price Cons You can get better gaming performance with a faster GPU (of course) Some hot air blows out the sides Price When Reviewed: $1,999.99 Best Prices Today: Retailer Price $2,459 View Deal $2479.99 View Deal Price comparison from over 24,000 stores worldwide CPU: Intel Core Ultra 9 275HX | GPU: Nvidia GeForce RTX 5070 RAM: 32GB DDR5 | Storage: 1TB PCIe 4.0 SSD | Screen: 16-inch, 2560×1600 IPS | Battery life: Just under 7 hours | Weight: 5.86 lbs Who should buy the Alienware 16X Aurora? The Alienware 16X Aurora delivers serious speed with its Intel Core Ultra 9 275HX CPU and RTX 5070 GPU. The 16-inch 2560×1600 display keeps every frame looking buttery smooth thanks to its 240Hz refresh rate, and its subtle Interstellar Indigo finish makes it look sharp in just about any setting, whether it’s in a dorm or office space. Alienware 16X Aurora: Further considerations Alienware packs in plenty of goodies here, like a crisp 1080p webcam (with Windows Hello facial recognition), Wi-Fi 7 for super fast connectivity, and a wide variety of ports. The full-size keyboard has a number pad and customizable backlighting. And you get nearly seven hours of battery life, which is awesome since long runtimes aren’t common in gaming laptops. Read our full Alienware 16X Aurora review Acer Nitro V 16 AI – Best budget gaming laptop Pros Large touchpad compared to alternatives 16-inch 1200p display at a low price Lots of physical connectivity Impressive battery life for a budget gaming laptop Cons Sub-par CPU performance Terrible audio quality from built-in speakers Wireless connectivity stuck on the Wi-Fi 6 standards Slightly more expensive laptops offer better value Price When Reviewed: $899 Best Prices Today: Retailer Price $1039.99 View Deal $1168.99 View Deal $1,229 View Deal Price comparison from over 24,000 stores worldwide CPU: AMD Ryzen 5 240 | GPU: Nvidia RTX 5050 RAM: 16GB DDR5-5600 | Storage: 512GB M.2 PCIe 4.0 SSD | Screen: 16-inch, 1920×1200, 180Hz IPS-LCD | Battery life: 8 to 12 hours | Weight: 5.38 lbs Who should buy the Acer Nitro V 16 AI? The Acer Nitro V 16 AI, which can occasionally be found as low as $629 at times, delivers great 1080p gaming performance–making it a great choice for gamers who don’t want to spend a ton. Its RTX 5050 outperforms other (older) entry-level graphics like the 4050, hitting an average 72 FPS in Cyberpunk 2077 . Surprisingly, for a gaming laptop, the battery life is surprisingly good, lasting eight to 12 hours with light use. Acer Nitro V 16 AI: Further considerations The 16-inch 1920×1200 IPS display offers more vertical space than standard 1080p panels, and the 180Hz refresh rate keeps things snappy during fast-paced games. The audio isn’t the best, but you can always hook up to external speakers. Overall, though, the Acer Nitro V 16 AI really hits the sweet spot between performance and affordability. Read our full Acer Nitro V 16 AI review Acer Swift 16 AI – Best college laptop Pros Sleek, sturdy design Sharp OLED screen Pleasantly tactile keyboard Good battery life Cons AI features still lacking Some keyboard keys too cramped Too many pre-loaded apps Price When Reviewed: $1,199.99 Best Prices Today: Retailer Price 16% off original price $999.99 View Deal $1066 View Deal $1239 View Deal Price comparison from over 24,000 stores worldwide CPU: Intel Core Ultra 7 256V | RAM: 16GB LPDDR5X | Storage : 1TB PCIe 4.0 SSD | Screen: 16-inch, 2880×1800 OLED | Battery life: 17.5 hours | Weight: 3.37 lbs Who should buy the Acer Swift 16 AI? If you need a laptop for college that won’t kill your back and doesn’t look boring, the Acer Swift 16 AI is worth checking out. It’s only 3.37 pounds, and the 16-inch OLED screen looks really sharp. Inside you get an Intel Core Ultra 7, Intel Arc graphics, 16GB of RAM, and a 1TB SSD. Not the fastest thing ever, but it handles schoolwork and big files without complaint. The 70Wh battery will get you through a full day of classes (we clocked it at 17.5 hours), and you can charge it via either of the USB-C Thunderbolt 4 ports. There’s also two USB-A ports, HDMI 2.1, Wi-Fi 7, and Bluetooth 5.4. Acer Swift 16 AI: Further considerations The OLED screen is such a lovely thing to behold–it’s bright, colorful, and sharp. The keyboard feels good for long typing sessions and, although the trackpad is on the smaller side and may feel cramped to some, it works fine for daily use. If you want a laptop that’s portable and won’t die on you halfway through the day, the Acer Swift 16 AI is the one to spring for. Read our full Acer Swift 16 AI review Microsoft Surface Pro – Best lightweight laptop Pros Compact and well-built Great office performance All Copilot Plus features available Good battery life Cons Narrow screen to work on No HDR support No charger included Price When Reviewed: $799.99 Best Prices Today: Retailer Price $949.99 View Deal $969.99 View Deal $979 View Deal $1049.99 View Deal $1049.99 View Deal $1049.99 View Deal Price comparison from over 24,000 stores worldwide View more prices CPU: Qualcomm Snapdragon X Plus | RAM: 16GB LPDDR5X | Storage : 512GB SSD | Screen: 12-inch, 2196×1464 IPS | Battery life: Up to 2 hours at full brightness, up to 19 hours with light use | Weight: 1.51 lbs Who should buy the Microsoft Surface Pro? If you’re always on the go — whether it’s the train, a coffee shop, or just hopping around the house — the Surface Pro is pretty much made for that. It’s super light (under two pounds!) and still powerful enough to handle all the usual stuff like emails and Zoom calls. With its Qualcomm Snapdragon X Plus CPU, it’s great for anyone who wants something that works like a laptop but feels like a tablet. You can doodle or get work done, all without feeling like you’re lugging around a heavy brick. Microsoft Surface Pro: Further considerations The smaller screen might not be great if you’re juggling a bunch of stuff all day, and there’s only two USB-C ports (so you’ll probably need a dock or something). Battery life can last a while, but honestly, it’s kind of all over the place. Expect around two hours at full brightness under heavy use or up to 19 hours with lighter tasks. Still, if your work mostly lives in the cloud and you value portability above raw power, this is the best ultraportable Windows device you can get right now. Read our full Microsoft Surface Pro 2025 review Dell 14S – Best laptop for battery life Pros Class-leading battery life Slick build Colorful and accurate display Good port selection Cons Dismal 3D performance Display isn’t very bright So-so performance for the money Price When Reviewed: $1,469 Best Prices Today: Retailer Price 13% off original price $1269.99 View Deal Price comparison from over 24,000 stores worldwide CPU: Intel Core Ultra 7 355 | RAM: 16GB LPDDR5x-7467 | Storage: 512GB PCIe 4.0 SSD (Kioxia EG7) | Screen: 14-inch, 1920×1200 OLED touchscreen | Graphics: Intel Graphics | Webcam: 2MP + IR camera | Weight: 3.28 lbs Who should buy the Dell 14S? If battery life is at the top of your list, the Dell 14S is hard to beat. It lasted nearly 36 hours in our offline video playback test–the longest runtime PCWorld has ever recorded from a laptop. If you normally spend days away from an outlet, this is the laptop to get. The Dell 14S doesn’t skimp on performance, either. You’re getting plenty of headroom for multitasking thanks to the Intel Core Ultra 7 355 processor, 16GB RAM, and Intel Graphics. This specific configuration also includes Intel Arc graphics, which provides a nice little boost in the graphics department. Dell 14S: Further considerations The OLED display is colorful and accurate, but its 1920×1200 resolution and 60Hz refresh rate aren’t exactly impressive when compared to other premium laptops. Graphics performance also depends on the configuration you’ve got. Lower-end models with standard Intel Graphics are noticeably weaker for creative work and light gaming. Read our full Dell 14S review Asus Chromebook Plus CX34 – Best Chromebook Pros Zippy processor performance Memorable keyboard A wide array of connectivity options Chic design Cons Battery life isn’t competitive The display’s 16:9 aspect ratio feels a little cramped Price When Reviewed: $499 Best Prices Today: Retailer Price $569 View Deal Price comparison from over 24,000 stores worldwide CPU: Intel Core i5-1335U | RAM: 8GB | Storage : 128GB (universal flash storage) | Screen size: 14-inch, 1920×1080 touchscreen | Battery life: 13 hours | Weight: 3.17 lbs Who should buy the Asus Chromebook Plus CX34? If you need a zippy Chromebook for everyday tasks, the Asus Chromebook Plus CX34 won’t let you down–it’s simple, reliable, and ready to handle whatever your day throws at it. This machine will easily crush your daily workflow thanks to its Intel i5 processor and 8GB of RAM. The 14-inch 1080p display also looks sharp, and the 1080p webcam is perfect for Zoom calls. Asus Chromebook Plus CX34: Further considerations While the Asus Chromebook Plus CX34 offers smooth performance and a pretty design, there are minor trade-offs to be aware of like the non-competitive battery life (13 hours). You’ll also need to be comfortable with ChromeOS. If you prefer Windows or macOS, we’d recommend looking elsewhere. Read our full Asus Chromebook Plus CX34 review Framework Laptop 13 – Best laptop for upgrading Pros Repairable and upgradeable Great keyboard Display is easy on the eyes Cons High up-front cost Battery life lags way behind Not quite seamless design Price When Reviewed: $1,946 Best Prices Today: Retailer Price Framework 56% off original price $849 View Deal Price comparison from over 24,000 stores worldwide CPU: AMD Ryzen AI 7 350 | RAM: 16GB DDR5-5600 | Storage : 1TB PCIe 4.0 SSD | Screen: 13.5-inch, 2880×1920 IPS | Battery life: Just over 11 hours | Weight: 2.99 lbs Who should buy the Framework Laptop 13? Need a laptop that’s super easy to upgrade and tough enough to stick around? The Framework Laptop 13 is where it’s at. You can swap out pretty much anything—RAM, storage, even the motherboard if you want! It runs on an AMD Ryzen AI 300 processor and is slim enough to toss in your bag and go wherever. Framework Laptop 13: Further considerations The price might sting a bit upfront, and the built-in graphics are okay for everyday stuff, but don’t expect much gaming performance. Battery life’s decent, but nothing groundbreaking. Read our full Framework Laptop 13 (2025) review Other good laptops we’ve tested Geekom GeekBook M16 : The GeekBook M16 is a solid budget productivity laptop with outstanding battery life and build quality, but its weak display and limited graphics performance hold it back from being a true all-rounder. Dell XPS 13 : Dell’s XPS 13 is a compelling budget laptop, even if it falls just slightly behind the MacBook Neo. Acer TravelMate P2 14 AI : The Acer TravelMate P2 14 AI is a good laptop. But there’s cheaper laptops out there that can deliver better performance, battery life, and value. Acer Chromebook Plus 516 : The Acer Chromebook Plus 516 isn’t much to look at, but it benefits from an Intel Core i3 chip with solid performance and, at times, low sale pricing. Laptops we don’t recommend Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 3i : Lenovo’s budget IdeaPad Slim 3i doesn’t quite offer as much as competing devices or even competing IdeaPads, though there’s noting inherently wrong with it. Dell 16S : Everything is more expensive now, but that doesn’t excuse the Dell 16S for lagging so far behind similarly priced contemporaries at just about every corner. Lenovo ThinkPad P16s Gen 4 : The Lenovo ThinkPad P16s Gen 4 is a typical workstation affair. It’s fairly potent but big, bulky, and pricey. Next to consumer laptops, its performance doesn’t impress, and new Panther Lake hardware threatens it at every turn. How we test laptops The PCWorld team puts each and every Windows laptop through a series of benchmarks that test GPU and CPU performance, battery life, and so on. The idea is to push the laptop to its limits and then compare it against others we’ve tested. Chromebooks, on the other hand, go through a series of web-based tests. For a much deeper look at our review methodology, check out how PCWorld tests laptops . Who curated this article? Hi, I’m Ashley Biancuzzo , and I oversee all laptop and Chromebook coverage at PCWorld. While you’ll see me review Chromebooks on occasion, I’m also deeply immersed in the broader world of consumer tech. I spend a lot of time writing and thinking about where laptops are headed–from AI and sustainable designs to long-term trends. When I’m not deep in the world of tech, you’ll probably find me gaming, getting lost in a book, or chilling with my rescue greyhound. How to choose the best laptop What’s the best laptop style? Regular ones are fine for everyday stuff. 2-in-1s are cool because the screen flips around. Chromebooks are cheap and good if you mostly do web browsing. How much power? Depends on what you’re doing. For basic web or email, an Intel Core i3 or Ryzen 3 works fine. If you’re into video editing or creative stuff, an i7/i9 or Ryzen 7/9 is better. And if you’re handling heavy 4K editing or lots of apps, a Ryzen 9 is your best bet. Discrete graphics vs. integrated graphics? Gamers and video editors need a legit graphics card—Nvidia, AMD, something with real muscle. But if all you’re doing is YouTube, emails, and Netflix, the built-in graphics won’t hold you back. How much RAM? RAM is more important than ever , especially with AI-powered features using more memory. 16GB is the sweet spot for most folks today. 8GB is fine for the basic stuff, but can quickly feeling limiting after a year or so. 32GB or more is ideal for gaming, heavy multitasking, and content creation. What’s the right display size? Doing video edits? Go bigger—15 or 17 inches helps a ton. For everyday use, 13 or 14 inches usually does the trick. Light enough to toss in your bag, not a pain to carry, and still plenty of space to get stuff done. Battery-life expectations If you’re gonna carry your laptop around, try to get one that lasts 10 to 12 hours on a charge. That’s usually enough for a long flight or a full day of classes. Some of the new Snapdragon laptops are even crushing that, with one going up to 25 hours thanks to their super-efficient chips . Just remember, bigger batteries usually mean heavier laptops. Laptop pricing guide A decent laptop usually runs $500 to $750. If money’s tight, a Chromebook or a basic work laptop under $500 will get you by. Push closer to $1,000 and you’ll start seeing nicer screens and more speed, but it really depends on what you need. Don’t forget the ports I like laptops with lots of ports so you don’t need adapters. Having both USB-C and USB-A is great. An HDMI port is especially useful for hooking up to an external monitor, especially if your laptop display just isn’t cutting it the way you want it to. FAQ 1. What is the best laptop? PCWorld calls the Acer Swift 16 AI the best overall laptop. It delivers fast, responsive performance thanks to Intel’s Panther Lake platform, handles multitasking without breaking a sweat, and packs impressive battery life for a 16-inch OLED machine, lasting around 18.5 hours in testing. 2. What is the best cheap laptop? The MacBook Neo is PCWorld’s favorite budget pick. It packs Apple’s A19 Pro chip, which delivers plenty of speed for everyday work and browsing. You also get a gorgeous 13-inch Liquid Retina display and a premium aluminum design. 3. What is the best gaming laptop? The Alienware 16X Aurora is a powerful gaming laptop that handles modern games with ease and makes them look amazing. It’s got an Intel Core Ultra 9 275HX CPU and RTX 5070 graphics, so performance is top-notch without going overboard on price. 4. When is the best time to buy a laptop? The best time to buy a laptop is usually during big sales events like Black Friday or Cyber Monday. Back-to-school season’s also good. 5. What is a 2-in-1 laptop? A 2-in-1 is a flexible laptop that can flip and fold, more or less–basically, the acrobat of the laptop world. Want to kick back and watch Netflix? Prop it up like a tent. Need to take notes at your next meeting? Fold the keyboard back and jot things down on the touchscreen. They’re a hit with students and creatives who want a bit of everything in one device. 6. What is a Copilot+ laptop? A Copilot+ laptop is a PC with AI built right in. It helps you draft emails, generate images, and more. Since the AI runs locally, AI performance should be snappier. But at the end of the day, it’s still just a normal laptop (more or less), with a little helper that makes life easier to manage. To qualify as a Copilot+ laptop, though, it needs an NPU that can meet 40 TOPS of performance.
